entries.clue: Jazz genre’s providing hits (4)

blocks.note: bop (bebop) is a style of jazz
the possessive S, read as a letter

annotation.surface: A music writer claims a jazz style is producing chart hits.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'hits' sound like chart successes; here it is the verb-noun for blows, which is what bops are.
annotation.definitionFit: A bop is a punch or blow, so bops are hits.

entries.clue: Attacks putting Belgium on edge, son (10)

indicatorNotes.putting: placing one piece in position beside the next
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, B sits on top of what follows

blocks.note: B is the international vehicle code for Belgium
the roadside is the edge of a road

annotation.surface: Military attacks that leave Belgium tense, with a son somehow involved.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On edge' reads as nervous, but 'on' is the placing word and 'edge' alone gives ROADSIDE.
annotation.definitionFit: A broadside is a full volley of fire, or a fierce verbal attack.

entries.clue: Camera-loving, goofy pooch: get in! (10)

indicatorNotes.goofy: silly and clumsy, so the letters are in a foolish order

annotation.surface: An owner calls a silly, camera-hogging dog back indoors.
annotation.walkthrough: The dog and the camera belong together in the picture, which hides that 'pooch get in' is simply letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Something photogenic looks good on camera, as if the camera loves it.

entries.clue: In France, thousands mobbing idiot in city on the Med (10)

indicatorNotes.In France: tells you to take the French word
indicatorNotes.mobbing: crowding round, so MILLES surrounds ARSE

blocks.note: mille is French for thousand; plural MILLES
an arse is British slang for a fool

annotation.surface: A crowd of thousands hounds a fool in a Mediterranean city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In France' looks like it locates the city, but it tells you to translate 'thousands'. The English spelling of the city keeps the final S that the French Marseille drops.
annotation.definitionFit: Marseilles is France's great port on the Mediterranean.

entries.clue: Having lost front of tome, fussily laminate one on bookshelves (1,1,5)

indicatorNotes.Having lost: tells you a letter is removed

blocks.note: first letter of tome, which is removed, leaving LAMINAE

annotation.surface: Someone fussily laminates the cover of a book on the shelf, damaging it.
annotation.walkthrough: The seven letters left after T goes are rearranged into the author's name. A A Milne wrote Winnie-the-Pooh, and so has a place on bookshelves.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an author is shelved by name, so a writer counts as 'one on bookshelves'.

entries.clue: Medical supports after run’s undergone change of direction (7)

indicatorNotes.undergone change of direction: a turn from right to left, so the letter R becomes L

annotation.surface: After a runner's injury makes him change course, he needs medical supports.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Change of direction' is literal: the direction letter R, for right, is replaced by L, for left.
annotation.definitionFit: Splints are rigid supports that hold an injured limb in place.

entries.clue: Ivanhoe, novel: almost perfect? Beats me! (1,4,2,4)

indicatorNotes.novel: new, so the letters are made new
indicatorNotes.almost: almost perfect is not quite perfect, so the word falls one letter short of complete

annotation.surface: Someone asked whether Ivanhoe is nearly a perfect novel shrugs and gives up.
annotation.walkthrough: Ivanhoe is Walter Scott's novel, so 'novel' looks like a description; it is the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are casual ways of saying you don't know.

entries.clue: In report, vegetable that’s prepared by whistleblower (4)

annotation.definitionNote: a relative clause standing for the noun it describes: something prepared by a whistleblower

indicatorNotes.In report: a report is something spoken and heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: the leek is a long onion-family vegetable

annotation.surface: A news report about a vegetable dish prepared by a whistleblower.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prepared' pulls toward cooking the vegetable; the whistleblower prepares a leak of documents.
annotation.definitionFit: A whistleblower releases secret information, which is a leak.

entries.clue: Second time Everyman’s shown up: stop! (4)

indicatorNotes.shown up: in a down clue, 'up' turns the piece to read bottom to top

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as ME

annotation.surface: The second time the crossword setter has appeared, someone cries stop.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself stands for ME, and this ME reads upward as EM.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as an imperative verb: you stem bleeding or a tide by halting its flow.

entries.clue: Woodwind member regularly going for broke (4)

blocks.note: the even letters of fOr BrOkE

annotation.surface: A woodwind player keeps going all out for broke.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going for broke' reads as a single idiom, but 'going' belongs to the indicator and only 'for broke' is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the double-reed oboe sits in the orchestra's woodwind section alongside flute and clarinet.

entries.clue: Bring together, in the morning, bits of seaweed, pal (10)

blocks.note: an alga is one of the simple plants that make up seaweed

annotation.surface: Instructions to gather seaweed with a friend on a morning beach walk.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make the clue read as a list of things to collect; each item is simply the next piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: merging companies or metals into one whole is uniting them.

entries.clue: Omit one of the Soup Dragon’s friends: goof! (4,1,7)

blocks.clueFragment: one of the Soup Dragon’s friends
blocks.note: the Soup Dragon lives with the Clangers, so one of them is a Clanger

annotation.surface: Leave out one of a children's-TV character's friends, which would be a blunder.
annotation.walkthrough: The Clangers was a British children's TV show about small knitted creatures on a planet with the Soup Dragon. To drop a clanger is British slang for making an embarrassing mistake.
annotation.definitionFit: Dropping a clanger means committing an obvious blunder, a goof.

entries.clue: An inspiration? Bold old university radical getting dainty snack (5-6)

blocks.note: a muse is a source of inspiration

annotation.surface: A bold old campus radical, once an inspiration, is now handed a tiny appetiser.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark makes 'An inspiration?' look like a comment; it is the first piece, A MUSE.
annotation.definitionFit: An amuse-bouche is a bite-sized appetiser served before a meal.

entries.clue: Puddings, good and bad consumed: nice feelings later (10)

indicatorNotes.consumed: eaten up, so the outer word takes the others inside

blocks.note: afters is British slang for dessert
low = poor, bad, as in low quality

annotation.surface: Puddings good and bad were eaten, and a warm contented feeling followed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Good and bad' sounds like a verdict on the puddings, but each word is a piece to be swallowed. In Britain 'pudding' and 'afters' both mean dessert.
annotation.definitionFit: An afterglow is the pleasant feeling left once something is over.

entries.clue: Misguided idealist embracing ‘alternative’ leaders (10)

indicatorNotes.Misguided: led wrongly, so the letters go astray
indicatorNotes.embracing: to embrace is to hug, so the rearranged letters wrap round the other piece

annotation.surface: A naive idealist supports alternative political leaders.
annotation.walkthrough: In British newspapers a leader is the editorial column, not a politician, which is what the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A leader, in British papers, is the editorial giving the paper's own opinion.

entries.clue: Kill 27? With tongs – that’s cold (3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: a cryptic hint describing the thing, rather than a synonym

blocks.note: to ice someone is slang for to kill them

annotation.surface: A gangster's order to kill, with tongs as the grim tool, called cold-blooded.
annotation.walkthrough: '27' looks like a reference to another clue, but the puzzle has no 27; it is just the number, a cube.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: tongs are what you use to drop cubes into a drink, and 'that's cold' completes the picture.

entries.clue: Dined and jeered (7)

blocks.note: to scoff is British slang for to eat greedily
to scoff at is to mock

annotation.surface: Someone ate and then mocked the host.
annotation.walkthrough: Scoff meaning to wolf down food is British informal usage.
annotation.definitionFit: Scoffed means both ate greedily and mocked.

entries.clue: Extremely vicious, insidious look expressing your enmity, primarily? (4,3)

annotation.definition: Extremely vicious, insidious look expressing your enmity, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: take the first letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: Extremely vicious, insidious look expressing your enmity
blocks.note: first letters of the seven words

annotation.surface: A description of a hostile, malicious glare.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: its first letters spell the answer, and it describes an evil eye.
annotation.definitionFit: The evil eye is a malevolent look believed to cause harm.

entries.clue: Lengthily describe one-time currency (7)

annotation.surface: Someone gives a long account of an old currency.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One-time currency' reads as a single dead money such as the franc, but the pound is still in use; 'one-time' is its own piece.
annotation.definitionFit: To expound is to explain something in detail.

entries.clue: Some yeti dies, tragically, being extremely trim (7)

indicatorNotes.Some: only part of the following words is used

annotation.surface: A sad scene: a yeti dies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tragically' looks like an anagram indicator, but it only supplies the final T.
annotation.definitionFit: Tidiest is the superlative of tidy, so extremely trim and neat.

entries.clue: Novelist to clasp – but regularly dropping – chihuahua? (7)

blocks.note: cLaSp, with c, a and p dropped
a chihuahua is a toy dog breed

annotation.surface: A novelist cuddling a tiny dog, which keeps slipping from his grasp.
annotation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'regularly dropping' look like the dog wriggling; it applies to 'clasp'. The question mark flags a chihuahua as an example of a toy.
annotation.definitionFit: Leo Tolstoy wrote War and Peace.

entries.clue: Ghastly Double German? (12)

blocks.note: the surface reads this as a dreadful look-alike; the setter means a ghostly double, a spectral twin
the surface makes it the person's nationality; it says the word for this spectre is itself German

annotation.surface: Someone meets an eerie look-alike of a German.
annotation.walkthrough: The word itself is German, doppel (double) plus Gänger (walker), so 'German' describes the word, not the person.
annotation.definitionFit: A doppelganger is a ghostly or uncanny double of a living person.

entries.clue: Dairy product with drug additive: for what reason? (4)

indicatorNotes.with: joining the drug to the other piece

annotation.surface: Someone asks why a dairy product has a drug added to it.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'for what reason?' look like a puzzled aside about the additive; it is the word the drug is slipped into. E for ecstasy is a standard crossword abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Whey is the watery part left when milk curdles.

entries.clue: Herb cycling for a long time (4)

indicatorNotes.cycling: the first letter moves round to the end

blocks.note: sage is a herb, and this is its back three letters, now leading
the front letter of the same herb, sent round to the end

annotation.surface: A herb out on a bike ride for hours.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For a long time' stands in for the bare adverb, as in 'I waited ages'.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: 'ages' used adverbially means a very long time, a hyperbole from the sense of historical eras.

entries.clue: Drunk romances eminent lawyers (4,6)

blocks.note: to court someone is to woo them

annotation.surface: A drunk woos distinguished lawyers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' can look like an anagram indicator, but there is nothing here to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: The High Courts are senior courts, bodies of eminent judges.

entries.clue: Star in river’s reflection (4)

blocks.note: the Avon is a British river

annotation.surface: A star seen mirrored in a river.
annotation.walkthrough: The Avon is the river through Stratford; reversed it gives NOVA.
annotation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares in brightness.

entries.clue: Indeed, strayed wildly in times gone by (10)

annotation.surface: Someone admits they wandered wildly in their past.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Indeed' looks like emphasis, but it is YES, the first piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative plural: 'yesterday' stretches from the day before to the past in general, as in the song.

entries.clue: Demands chores when temperature’s dropped (4)

indicatorNotes.dropped: something dropped is let fall and lost, so T falls out of the word

annotation.surface: When the weather cools, someone demands more household chores.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temperature's dropped' sounds like weather, but it means the letter T is taken away.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: someone who asks a price or a favour is demanding it.
